items.actClause:
AN ACT to amend the public health law, in relation to definitions and
conforming changes pertaining to anatomical gifts; and to repeal certain
provisions of such law relating thereto (Part A); to amend the public health
law, in relation to changes in anatomical gift consent (Part B); and to amend
the public health law, in relation to changes in anatomical gift revocation
and amendment (Part C)
items.lawCode: Amd §§4300, 4301 & 4305, rpld §4303 sub 5, Pub Health L
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S1342

SPONSOR: RIVERA
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the public health law, in relation to definitions and
conforming changes pertaining to anatomical gifts; and to repeal certain
provisions of such law relating thereto (Part A); to amend the public
health law, in relation to changes in anatomical gift consent (Part B);
and to amend the public health law, in relation to changes in anatomical
gift revocation and amendment (Part C)

 
PURPOSE:

To amend the Public Health Law, in relation to bringing New York's defi-
nition and consent rules governing anatomical gifts into line with the
Uniform Anatomical Gift Act.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section one establishes the legislative intent.

Section two explains the structure of the various parts of the bill.

Part A:

Section one amends section 4300 of the Public Health Law to conform
definitions of terms to definitions in the Uniform Anatomical Gift Act.

Section two repeals subdivision 5 of section 4303 of the Public Health
Law, as this subdivision is placed into section 4301 instead.

Section three establishes the effective date.

Part B:

Section one amends section 4301 of the Public Health Law to provide that
if there is a group of family members in a category that is authorized
to make a decision about an anatomical gift by a deceased relative, the
group's decision is by the majority (a tie would not be sufficient to
make the gift); and conforms with definitions as amended in Part A
section one.

Section two establishes the effective date.

Part C:

Section one amends section 4305 of the Public Health Law to enact the
same provision as in Part B, Section one, for a decision to alter an
anatomical gift (a tie would not be sufficient to amend) and for revoca-
tion of an anatomical gift (a tie being sufficient to revoke); and
conforms with definitions as amended in Part A Section one.

Section two establishes the effective date.

Section three establishes the severability.

Section four establishes the effective date.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

The purpose of this legislation is to enact changes to follow the
Uniform Anatomical Gift Act (UAGA) as proposed by the National Confer-
ence of Commissioners on Uniform State Laws.

The UAGA was enacted in 1968 following the first successful heart trans-
plant, and was revised in 1987 and 2006 to clarify consent rules and
other processes. Most states have enacted the recent changes, but New
York has not.

Only New York and Pennsylvania have consent rules under which any one of
a group of family members can block an anatomical gift, rather than
using a majority rule process. For example, under current New York law,
if a parent of five children dies, the deceased's wishes are not known
and four of the five children wish to make an anatomical gift, the one
lone objector can block the gift.

This bill would instead implement a majority rule among the individuals
in whichever class has priority to make the decision (e.g., among the
decedent's children, grandchildren, siblings), in compliance with the
UAGA. In the event of a tie, the gift cannot be made. The bill also
provides that in a majority ruling for an amendment of an anatomical
gift, a tie would not be sufficient to amend; however, in a majority
ruling for revocation of an anatomical gift, a tie would be sufficient
to revoke the gift.

While New York has made recent improvements to our organ donation rules
and participation rates, we still face a severe organ shortage.  It is
estimated that bringing New York's anatomical gift consent rules into
agreement with UAGA would produce an additional 100 donors for a total
of 200-300 additional organs available over five years.

 
LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New bill.

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

None.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect immediately.
